Rib fractures are common and often are managed nonsurgically; however, in severely
injured patients, rib fractures may play a major role in mortality and morbidity. Surgical
management of these fractures is relatively new, and the indications for surgical
management are expected to change as additional studies become available.
Epidemiology
Most rib fractures are relatively benign and heal without major morbidity.
Ribs 7 through 10 are fractured most often.
Rib fractures may be a sign of severe injury, and a greater number of fractured ribs correlates
with increased morbidity and mortality.
As many as 300,000 individuals are evaluated annually for rib fractures, 7% of whom require
hospitalization for medical and/or surgical management.
Rib fractures occur in as many as 10% of hospitalized trauma patients, with mortality rates
ranging from 3% to 13%.
Patients with advanced age, osteoporosis, or osteopenia have an increased risk for rib
fractures and typically have a greater number and increased severity of fractures.
Elderly patients with rib fractures have poorer outcomes than those younger than 65 years in
terms of mortality, length of hospital stay, length of intensive care unit (ICU) stay, and
ventilator days. In a study of elderly patients, the mortality rate was 19% in those with three to
four rib fractures and 33% in those with more than six rib fractures.
Flail chest, typically defined as three or more consecutive ribs fractured in more than one
place, causes paradoxical movement of the affected flail chest wall segment.
Rib fractures and flail chest may cause severe pain and frequently are associated with
concomitant injuries, such as pneumothorax, hemopneumothorax, and/or pulmonary
contusions. Flail chest is associated with a mortality rate as high as 15%.

Flail chest, typically defined as three or more consecutive ribs fractured and/or

chest wall segment. Rib fractures and flail chest may cause severe pain and inhibit
breathing and frequently are associated with concomitant injuries, such as
pneumothorax, hemopneumothorax, and/or pulmonary contusions. They also account
for a substantial number of complications2 and contribute to long-term disability and
loss of work.3 In addition, flail chest is associated with a mortality rate as high as 15%.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The thoracic cage consists of 12 pairs of ribs. The ribs are numbered 1 to 12 according to the
corresponding thoracic vertebra to which they connect posteriorly (Figure 1).

point at which the rib has its greatest degree of curvature.
The osseous components of ribs do not extend anteriorly to the sternum. Rather, the anterior

several centimeters. Most ribs are attached directly or indirectly to the sternum via their costal
cartilage.
The inferior portion of the rib has a channel, the sulcus costae, with an artery, vein, and

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The thoracic cage consists of 12 pairs of ribs. The ribs are numbered 1 to 12 according to
the corresponding thoracic vertebra to which they connect posteriorly. The posterior
end is called the head. A series of gliding or arthrodial joints are formed by the
articulations of the heads of the typical ribs (ie, the costocentral articulations) with the
facets on the contiguous margins of the bodies of the thoracic vertebrae and with the
intervertebral fibrocartilages between them. Ribs 1, 11, and 12 articulate with a single
vertebra. Lateral to the head is the narrowed neck. A small eminence located on the
posterior rib surface, called the tubercle, articulates with the facet located on the
transverse process of the same numbered vertebra. The remainder of the rib is referred
to as the body or shaft. Just lateral to the tubercle is the angle, the point at which the rib
has its greatest degree of curvature. The osseous components of the ribs do not extend
anteriorly to the sternum. Rather, the anterior end of each rib ends with costal cartilage,
which is made of hyaline cartilage and may extend for several centimeters. Most ribs are
attached directly or indirectly to the sternum via their costal cartilage. The inferior
portion of the rib has a channel, called the sulcus costae, with an artery, vein, and
intercostal nerve. This has implications for approaches to each rib in the surgical
management of fractures and the placement of a chest tube.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Most rib fractures result from direct injury to the chest wall secondary to blunt or penetrating
trauma.
A single impact may result in multiple fractures of the same rib and fractures of multiple ribs.
Fractures typically occur directly at the site of impact and/or at the angle (ie, posterolateral
bend) at which the rib is weakest.
Rib fractures also may be pathologic.
Cancers that commonly metastasize to bone, such as prostate, breast, and renal cancers,
frequently appear early in the ribs.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Most rib fractures result from direct injury to the chest wall secondary to blunt or
penetrating trauma. A single impact may cause multiple fractures in the same rib and
fractures of multiple ribs. Fractures typically occur directly at the site of impact and/or at
the angle (ie, posterolateral bend) at which the rib is weakest. Rib fractures also may be
pathologic. Cancers that commonly metastasize to bone, such as prostate, breast, and
renal cancers, frequently appear early in the ribs. Stress fractures may be observed in
patients with a chronic cough and in athletes, such as rowers, golfers, and throwing
athletes. Because the first rib is subjected to unique forces, it is particularly susceptible
to stress fractures in overhead throwing athletes.
Risk Factors
Trauma patients with advanced age, osteoporosis, or osteopenia have an increased risk for rib
fractures and typically have a greater number of and more severe fractures.
Associated Injuries
Rib fractures and flail chest injuries from high-energy trauma often are associated with
complications.
Fractures of ribs 1, 2, or 3 may be associated with mediastinal injury, particularly to the aorta,
and injury to the brachial plexus and the subclavian vessels; such fractures have been
associated with increased mortality in some observational studies.
First rib fractures are associated with greater overall severity (Injury Severity Score >15) and
life-threatening internal injury (including injury to the brain, spine, lungs, and pelvis)
independent of mechanism of injury, patient age, or patient sex.

Associated Injuries
Rib fractures and flail chest injuries caused by high-energy trauma often are associated
with other injuries. Fractures of ribs 1, 2, or 3 may be associated with mediastinal injury,
particularly to the aorta, and injury to the brachial plexus and the subclavian vessels. In
some observational studies , they also have been associated with increased mortality.
First rib fractures are associated with greater overall severity (Injury Severity Score >15)
and life-threatening internal injury (including injuries to the brain, spine, lungs, and
pelvis) independent of mechanism of injury, patient age, or patient sex. Intra-abdominal
organ injuries are more common in patients with fractures of ribs 9 through 12, with
hepatic and splenic injuries being most common.
Injury Classification
No formal classification of rib fractures is currently used.

Injury Classification
Rib fractures are classified in descriptive terms based on laterality, location, and
displacement (eg, fracture of posterolateral aspect of left rib 7 with 2 cm of shortening
and 100% displacement”). Multiple rib fractures generally are classified as a flail segment
if three or more consecutive ribs are fractured in more than one place.

Patient History
Most patients with rib fractures present with an obvious high-energy mechanism of
injury, such as a motor vehicle collision. Patients with rib fractures who have not
sustained high-energy trauma typically describe a history of minor or moderate blunt
trauma to the chest wall or a specific repetitive activity that resulted in an insidious onset
of pain. The most common symptom of rib fractures is pain. In patients with stress
fractures, pain also can be elicited via reproduction of the inciting activity, such as
bearing down, sneezing, coughing, or laughing.
Physical Examination
Visible bruising may appear around a fractured rib; however, this is not common.
Physical examination findings strongly suggestive of a rib fracture include point tenderness
on a specific rib or focal tenderness caused by compression of the rib cage distant from the
site of pain.
Pneumothorax may present as diminished breath sounds and possibly subcutaneous
crepitus because of subcutaneous emphysema.
Flail chest occurs if three or more adjacent ribs are fractured in at least two places, creating
one floating segment composed of several ribs and the soft tissues between them; this
unstable section of chest wall exhibits paradoxical motion, moving in the opposite direction
of the uninjured, normal-functioning chest wall with breathing.
Similar to stress fractures of other bones, rib stress fractures are associated with with a
gradual onset of activity-related chest wall pain. Initially, the pain occurs only with the inciting

Physical Examination
Bruising may be visible around the fractured rib; however, this is not common. Physical
examination findings strongly suggestive of rib fracture include point tenderness on a
specific rib or focal tenderness caused by compression of the rib cage distant from the
site of pain. Bony crepitus also may be present. Pneumothorax may present as
diminished breath sounds and possibly subcutaneous crepitus because of subcutaneous
emphysema. Flail chest occurs if three or more adjacent ribs are fractured in at least two
places, creating one floating segment composed of several ribs and the soft tissues
between them; this unstable section of chest wall exhibits paradoxical motion, moving in
the opposite direction of uninjured, normal-functioning chest wall with breathing. This
can be visualized during the physical examination. Similar to stress fractures of other
bones, rib stress fractures are associated with a gradual onset of activity-related chest
wall pain. Initially, the pain occurs only with the inciting activity and progressing to pain
with deep breathing or simple movements, such as rolling over in bed or reaching
overhead.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Standard PA and lateral chest radiographs are adequate to identify some rib fractures;
however, their overall sensitivity is poor (Figure 2).
The sensitivity of dedicated rib radiographs for the detection of rib fractures is higher than that
of standard chest radiographs because they involve a bone exposure (ie, entailing higher levels
of radiation). Rib radiographs also include oblique views of the chest wall, which are not part of
a standard chest radiographic series (Figure 3).

Computed Tomography
In trauma patients, rib fractures are commonly identified on CT scans during assessment for
internal injuries. Suspected intrathoracic and/or intra-abdominal injuries usually are confirmed
via CT of the chest/abdomen/pelvis.
Two-dimensional and three-dimensional (Figure 4) CT reconstruction images are valuable in
assessing the amount of fracture displacement and chest wall deformity and, therefore,
determining management. Caution should be exercised in assessing coronal, sagittal, and
three-dimensional CT reconstruction images because volume averaging may lead to
smoothening out of fracture lines and, ultimately, missed fractures. Therefore, conventional
axial CT scan should always be evaluated.

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Rib fractures and flail chest may be treated via pain management.
Patients are encouraged to use an incentive spirometer aggressively, and pulmonary/chest
therapy may be beneficial.
Supplemental oxygen is used, depending on the patient’s symptoms and oxygen saturation
level.
The Eastern Association for the Surgery of Trauma and the Trauma Anesthesiology Society
conditionally recommend epidural and multimodal analgesia for patients with blunt
thoracic trauma.
Options include the following:
Narcotic agents
Oral or intravenous acetaminophen
Oral ibuprofen
Gabapentin
Thoracic epidural catheter (limited in the setting of deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis)
Continuous infusion of local anesthetic agent
Liposomal bupivacaine rib block
Paravertebral block or continuous catheter

encouraged to use an incentive spirometer aggressively, and pulmonary/chest therapy
may be beneficial. Supplemental oxygen may be used, depending on the patient’s
symptoms and oxygen saturation level. The Eastern Association for the Surgery of

Surgical Management
Indications
Indications for rib fracture repair4,5
Flail chest
Multiple rib fractures with bicortical displacement
Uncontrolled pain with failed nonsurgical management
Chest wall deformity/defect
Chest wall crush injury with collapsed structure of the chest wall and loss of thoracic
volume (Figure 5)
Severely displaced, multiple rib fractures or tissue defect that may result in permanent
deformity or pulmonary hernia
Severely displaced fractures that are substantially impeding lung expansion or rib fractures
that are impaling the lung
Patient who is expected to survive other injuries
Symptomatic rib fracture nonunion
Evidence of fracture nonunion on CT scans
Patient who reports persistent, symptomatic fracture movement

Indications
As of October 2020, no published prospective, randomized, controlled trials have
compared rib fixation with modern critical care via epidural or paravertebral analgesia
and chest physiotherapy in patients without flail chest; however, according to expert
opinion and prospective and retrospective studies, indications for surgical rib fixation
have expanded, with the goal of improving mortality, pulmonary function, pain,
deformity, and chest wall mechanics.4,5 Indications for rib fracture repair include flail
chest (three or more consecutive rib fractures in two or more places), multiple rib
fractures with bicortical displacement, uncontrolled pain with failed nonsurgical
management, chest wall deformity and/or defect, and symptomatic rib fracture
nonunion.
Contraindications
Contraindications for rib fracture fixation5
Hemodynamic instability
Traumatic brain injury (Glasgow Coma Scale score <11)
Infection: pleural empyema, mediastinitis, severe pneumonia

Spinal or pelvic fractures that must be stabilized before rib fixation

Contaminated surgical field

Techniques/Procedures
Preoperative Planning
If the sequence of plating depends on the need to reposition the patient, all ribs that are
accessible via the main surgical approach are stabilized initially.
If bilateral rib plating is planned, the more severely injured side is addressed first.
Surgical Approaches
Lateral thoracotomy
For anterolateral and posterolateral fractures, patients are placed in the lateral decubitus
position, and a lateral thoracotomy is performed.
The serratus muscle fibers are split in line to expose the fractured ribs.
Often, two or more separate windows are required, with possible fixation of two to three ribs
per window. The long thoracic nerve and artery on the lateral border of the serratus and the
thoracodorsal nerve and artery on the undersurface of the latissimus must be protected.
For posterolateral deep dissection, two approaches have been described.
The interval between the latissimus, trapezius, and inferior scapular border (triangle of
auscultation) may be used or the latissimus may be split in line with its fibers, depending on
the location of the fractured ribs.
Major muscle dissection should be avoided to preserve as much respiratory function as
possible.
Posterior paramedian approach
Posterior rib fractures are managed via a posterior paramedian approach.
The patient is placed in the lateral decubitus position with the arm draped free and placed
on a well-padded Mayo stand.
A vertical linear incision is made parallel to the spinous processes, centered over the
fractured ribs.

Deep dissection is carried out in the interval between the latissimus, the trapezius, and the
inferior scapular border (triangle of auscultation), exposing the underlying erector spinae
muscle.
The erector spinae is then elevated toward the midline to expose the posteriorly fractured
ribs.
Inframammary approach
Anterior fractures and costochondral dislocations are managed via the inframammary
approach. The patient is placed in the supine position, with arms placed at 90° to the thorax.
The arm need not be prepared into the surgical field.
A horizontal incision is made along the inframammary crease inferior to the pectoralis major.
Deep dissection is carried out under the pectoralis major, exposing the serratus anterior
fibers and the costochondral junctions as necessary.
The fibers of the serratus are split in line to expose the underlying ribs. To attain adequate
caudal exposure, splitting of the external oblique fibers may be necessary.
Minimally invasive approach
The thoracic literature describes rib fracture fixation via video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery
and minimal thoracic incisions; however, these techniques are not available to orthopaedic
surgeons.
Minimally invasive power drills and screwdrivers that drill and screw at a 90° angle allow the
surgeon to reach and place screws farther away without creating a new incision or new
dissection plane.

With the inframammary approach, anterior fractures and costochondral dislocations are
accessed with the patient placed in the supine position with the arms placed at 90° to
the thorax. The arm need not be prepared into the field. A horizontal incision is made
along the inframammary crease inferior to the pectoralis major, and deep dissection is

costochondral junctions as necessary. The fibers of the serratus are then split in line to
expose the underlying ribs. To attain adequate caudal exposure, splitting of the external
oblique fibers may be necessary.
According to the thoracic literature, in a minimally invasive procedure, rib fracture
fixation is performed via video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery and minimal thoracic
incisions; however, these techniques are not available to orthopaedic surgeons.
Minimally invasive power drills and screwdrivers that drill and screw at a 90° angle allow
the surgeon to reach and place screws farther away without creating a new incision or
new dissection plane.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
After the fractures have been exposed, reduction is straightforward. Fractures typically are
reduced with the use of two pairs of point-to-point reduction forceps to grasp each side of the
fracture.

Before fracture reduction, a small incision is made in the intercostal space over the superior
aspect of the affected rib (ie, to prevent injury to the intercostal neurovascular bundle). A
caliper is then inserted to determine rib thickness, the required depth of drilling, and screw
length.
Drill bits of varying lengths with stops can prevent plunging and injury to the pneumothorax
and lung.
Low-profile (1.5-mm), straight and precontoured titanium locking plates of various lengths,
locking screws, and intramedullary splints also are available. Plates typically are used.
Rib fractures posterior and close to the midline are more difficult to adequately fix because of
their proximity to the transverse processes; adequate fixation may not be possible on the
medial side of the fracture. In more posterior and medial fractures, intramedullary splints may
be more useful for this reason.

the pneumothorax and lung. Low-profile (1.5-mm), straight and pre-contoured titanium
locking plates of various lengths, locking screws, and intramedullary splints also are
available. Plates are most commonly used.
Rib fractures posterior and close to the midline are more difficult to adequately fix
because of their proximity to the transverse processes; therefore, adequate fixation may
not be possible on the medial side of the fracture. In more posterior and medial
fractures, intramedullary splints may be useful for this reason.

Surgery is an increasingly accepted approach to manage rib fractures and flail chest, with
many reports of improved patient outcomes compared with nonsurgical management.
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have demonstrated that surgical repair of rib fractures
and flail chest reduces the rates of pneumonia and chest deformity, the use of tracheostomy,
the duration of mechanical ventilation, the length of ICU and hospital stays, and treatment
costs and improves health-related outcomes.
In addition, mortality was lower in patients with flail chest treated surgically (relative risk, 0.44;
95% confidence interval, 0.28 to 0.69).6,7
Currently, no strong evidence supports improved mortality in patients without flail chest who
undergo rib fixation.

Outcomes
Surgical management of rib fractures and flail chest is increasingly accepted, with many
reports of improved patient outcomes compared with nonsurgical management.
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses have demonstrated that surgical repair of rib
fractures and flail chest reduces the rates of pneumonia and chest deformity, the use of
tracheostomy, the duration of mechanical ventilation, the length of ICU and hospital
stays, and treatment costs and improves health-related outcomes.6,7 In two meta-
analyses, mortality rates were decreased in patients with flail chest who were treated
surgically (relative risk, 0.44; 95% confidence interval, 0.28 to 0.69;6 and odds ratio, 0.31;
95% confidence interval, 0.20 to 0.487). Currently, no strong evidence supports improved
mortality rates in patients without flail chest who undergo rib fixation.
Complications
Nonunion
Persistent chest wall pain for 3 months or more after diagnosis of rib fracture or blunt injury to
the chest should prompt workup for fracture nonunion.
Repair is undertaken in the usual fashion; however, a bone graft typically used to augment the
healing process. Options include an iliac crest autograft or iliac crest aspiration mixed with
allograft (Video 1).
